Daily calorie calculator

How many calories you burn a day, and how many to eat to lose or gain weight slowly. Free, in the page, nothing sent anywhere.

Updated: 8 November 2026 · By Fotocal, Madrid · How we calculate

Sex

Choose woman or man.

Enter an age between 18 and 90.

Enter a height between 130 and 230 cm.

Enter a weight between 35 and 250 kg.

Choose what your day is like.

How is it worked out?

Your daily burn is your basal metabolism (Mifflin-St Jeor equation) times your activity: ×1.2 sedentary, ×1.375 light, ×1.465 moderate, ×1.55 active and ×1.725 very active. Workouts are not counted here: add them on the days you do them. The details are below.

Quick answer: A 35-year-old woman of 165 cm and 70 kg who is on her feet sometimes burns about 1,918 kcal a day; to lose half a kilo a week she needs about 1,439 kcal. Your number depends on your sex, age, height, weight and activity: enter them above and the calculator uses the Mifflin-St Jeor equation, like the app.

How it is calculated

In two steps. First the basal metabolic rate (BMR), what you burn at rest, with the Mifflin-St Jeor equation (1990), the one dietetics reviews find most accurate for healthy adults:

BMR = 10 × kg + 6.25 × cm − 5 × age + 5 (man) / − 161 (woman)

Then it is multiplied by a factor for your day-to-day, not counting workouts: 1.2 if you sit most of the day, 1.375 if you are on your feet sometimes, 1.465 if mostly standing, 1.55 if you move all day and 1.725 for hard physical work. The result is your maintenance, your total daily energy expenditure or TDEE.

To lose weight, the calculator takes off what 0.25 or 0.5 kg a week takes (7,700 kcal per kilo, spread over 7 days), but never more than 25% of your maintenance, and it never goes below 1,200 kcal for a woman or 1,500 for a man. These are the rules the Fotocal app uses, so the number here is the one you will see there.

A worked example

A 35-year-old woman, 165 cm and 70 kg, on her feet sometimes: BMR = 700 + 1,031.25 − 175 − 161 = 1,395 kcal. Times 1.375 gives a maintenance of 1,918 kcal. Losing half a kilo a week would need 550 kcal less, but that is more than 25% of what she burns, so the cut stays at 480: her target is 1,438 kcal. For a quarter of a kilo, 1,643 kcal.

A 35-year-old man, 178 cm and 85 kg, who moves all day burns about 2,778 kcal; with 550 less, 2,228 kcal a day, he loses half a kilo a week.

What to do with this number

Treat it as a starting point, not the truth: any formula is off by around 10% for a given person. Eat what it gives you for two or three weeks, logging everything, and watch your weekly average on the scale. If it does not move and you wanted to lose, cut 100 or 200 kcal more; if you lose faster than 1% of your weight a week, eat a little more. To split the number into protein, fat and carbs, use the macro calculator; to see how long it takes, the calorie deficit calculator.

To know what you really eat, it helps to know the calories of everyday Spanish food: a serving of tortilla de patatas, a plate of paella, lentil stew or a morning café con leche (those pages are in Spanish).

How many calories should I eat a day to keep my weight?

Your maintenance calories: what you burn. Eat that and your weight stays where it is. It depends on your sex, age, height, weight and what your day is like, so this table is only a guide for two specific people: a woman of 1.65 m and 65 kg and a man of 1.78 m and 80 kg. These are estimates from the Mifflin-St Jeor equation; for your own number, use the calculator above.

Mifflin-St Jeor or Harris-Benedict?

They are two equations for the same thing, basal metabolic rate. Harris-Benedict dates from 1919 and was revised in 1984; Mifflin-St Jeor is from 1990 and is the one this calculator and the app use. For the woman in the example (35 years, 165 cm, 70 kg), Mifflin-St Jeor gives 1,395 kcal at rest and revised Harris-Benedict 1,455: about 60 kcal more. The gap is small, but it explains why two calculators do not always agree.

Frequently asked questions

How many calories should I eat a day to lose weight?

Your maintenance minus a moderate cut: what a quarter or half a kilo a week takes, never more than 25% of what you burn. The calculator gives you both numbers. If you land below 1,200 kcal (women) or 1,500 (men), do not go lower without a health professional: slow the pace instead.

Is this the same as TDEE?

Yes. TDEE stands for total daily energy expenditure: what you burn in a day counting your basal metabolism, digestion and all your movement. Here we call it maintenance, because it is the number at which you neither lose nor gain.

Why does another calculator give me a different number?

Because it uses another equation (Harris-Benedict usually gives more) or other activity factors. None gets your exact number: the typical error for one person is around 10%. Take the result as a starting point and adjust it with the scale after two or three weeks.

Do I count exercise in the activity level?

No. The factor describes your day-to-day: work, commuting, chores. Exercise is added separately on the days you do it, which is how the app does it. Count it in both places and you count it twice.

Does it give the same number as the Fotocal app?

Yes, for the same inputs. It uses the same equations and the same limits: the activity factor, the 25% cap and the 1,200 and 1,500 kcal floors. In the app you can also set a target weight and a date.

How many calories do I burn a day at rest?

That is your basal metabolic rate: 58 to 83% of what you burn in a day, depending on how much you move. The woman in the example burns 1,395 kcal at rest and 1,918 in total. The BMR calculator gives you yours.

Sources

  • Mifflin MD, St Jeor ST et al. "A new predictive equation for resting energy expenditure in healthy individuals". Am J Clin Nutr 1990; 51(2): 241-247. View source
  • Roza AM, Shizgal HM. "The Harris Benedict equation reevaluated: resting energy requirements and the body cell mass". Am J Clin Nutr 1984; 40(1): 168-182 (the revised Harris-Benedict equation, used only in the comparison). View source
  • Wishnofsky M. "Caloric equivalents of gained or lost weight". Am J Clin Nutr 1958; 6(5): 542-546 (about 7,700 kcal per kilo). View source
